proposals.relationship: Trouillot credits Mintz’s knowledge with improving the Columbus chapter of Silencing the Past.
proposals.evidence_note: Own acknowledgments xvi explicitly identifies substantive help to chapter4. Joint Bonilla/Beckett/Fernando2021,27 independently situates his graduate-adviser relationship and shared Caribbean/peasant research while preserving Trouillot’s independent argument. Specific primary manuscript contribution, not influence inferred from employment or sole authorship of Trouillot’s thinking.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot uses Appadurai’s account of constraints on debating the past to argue that historical narratives require credibility.
proposals.evidence_note: Own8/n8 explicitly endorses rules concerning authority, continuity, depth and interdependence in1981ThePastasaScarceResource. This supports a particular history/fiction argument, not agreement with every proposed universal or fresh verification of the original article. Appadurai also appears in collective acknowledgments xviii–xix.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot includes Pocock among contributors whose leads, comments or documents made a substantive difference to Silencing the Past.
proposals.evidence_note: Own xviii–xix collective acknowledgment describes several possible forms of contribution and explicitly says results were not always intended by contributors. It does not assign a particular comment to Pocock, certify whole-manuscript reading, establish agreement or claim formal training.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot draws on Todorov when distinguishing historical truth claims from fiction and fabrication.
proposals.evidence_note: Own5/n2 and6–8/n5 use LesMoralesdelhistoire1991,129–169;157/n1 includes it among works helping chart a route between positivist and constructivist poles. Later79/n9 uses Todorov on rights of man/citizen. Selected manifestations and scope, not sole intellectual origin or fresh reading of Todorov’s book.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot acknowledges The Eighteenth Brumaire among works informing his route beyond one-sided accounts of historicity.
proposals.evidence_note: Own157/n1 explicitly includes Marx with Chesnaux/Ferro/deCerteau/Cohen/Guha/Pomian/Schaff/Todorov, with influence not always registered by mechanical citations;1926 English manifestation listed. Daut2021,135–144 specifically warns against reducing his Haitian intellectual genealogy to Marx. This narrow acknowledgment neither establishes exclusive inspiration nor makes Haitian political analysis dependent on a European source.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot credits de Certeau’s work as a resource for examining the production of historical narratives.
proposals.evidence_note: Own157/n1 names LEcriture1975 among resources, while22/161n26 specifically recognizes it with Cohen/Ferro as an exception to theories that neglect concrete production. His19–22/161n22 also questions restricting analysis to professional historians. Specific positive contribution with limits, not whole-model adoption or personal collaboration.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot names Guha’s “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency” among resources for escaping one-sided theories of historicity.
proposals.evidence_note: Own157/n1 explicitly names Guha1983SubalternStudies2 in the collective account of intellectual debts, including those not mechanically cited. Does not establish formal training, direct correspondence or dependence of all four moments on Guha; original essay not freshly read.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot uses Foucault’s warning to ask how power works in producing history, as well as who exercises it.
proposals.evidence_note: Own28/n32 quotes the particular1978Boncenne interview as edited by LawrenceD.Kritzman in1988PoliticsPhilosophyCulture,103. Specific methodological resource, not proof all his power analysis derives from Foucault. Daut2021,135–146/154 contests such reductive reception and emphasizes Haitian antecedents; original interview uncollated.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot challenges White’s earlier constructivist treatment of historical truth and explicitly acknowledges White’s later qualification.
proposals.evidence_note: Own12–13 and159–160/nn15–16 argues that Holocaust narratives cannot be reduced to legitimation alone; distinguishes TheContentoftheForm from1992HistoricalEmplotmentandtheProblemofTruth, in SaulFriedländer’s edited volume. Trouillot’s attributed interpretation, not a claim White denied the Holocaust or retained an unchanged position; originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot uses Curtin’s Atlantic slave-trade estimates in comparing slavery’s scale across the Americas.
proposals.evidence_note: Own17–18/160n18 cites1969Census for imported-slave figures while acknowledging partial updates and arguing magnitude does not automatically determine later historical relevance. Later173n50 cites French slave-trade figures. Resource use, not fresh certification of each dated estimate, equivalence of suffering or direct reply to every later criticism of Curtin.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot cites Foner’s Reconstruction in questioning whether slavery automatically supplied a fixed burden for later generations.
proposals.evidence_note: Own18–19/160–161n20 pairs Foner1988 with DuBois1898/BlackReconstruction in the particular discussion of post-emancipation understandings. A bounded cited analytical resource, not statement Foner endorsed every hemispheric comparison or fresh complete-book reading.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot uses Du Bois’s writings to historicize debates over slavery’s relevance after emancipation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own18–19/160–161nn20–21 cites SomeEffortsofAmericanNegroes1898 and1962BlackReconstruction manifestation alongside other authors. Separately98 identifies DuBois with HenryAdams as exceptions to neglect of Haiti, but that praise alone is not a fresh source-use finding. No sole origin, transcription of all DuBois positions or claim to have read his complete books.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot criticizes Hobsbawm’s marginal treatment of the Haitian Revolution while praising his skill as a historian of the era.
proposals.evidence_note: Own98–99/173n48 identifies brief mentions in TheAgeofRevolution1962,93/115 and argues that even left historiography can reproduce archival silences. Not literal total absence, conscious personal racism or a claim that declared politics alone determines omissions. Body99 gives an inconsistent title/date range; n48 and actual1962 work are distinguished without independently certifying his count of mentions.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot draws on Bourdieu’s definition of the unthinkable to analyze the conceptual challenge of the Haitian Revolution.
proposals.evidence_note: Own82–83/169n19 quotes LeSenspratique1980,14 and gives additional pages for everyday/social-science uses. Specific conceptual resource situated in Trouillot’s Caribbean historical argument, not sole origin of his work, independent validation of all claims about contemporaries or fresh reading of Bourdieu’s entire book.

proposals.relationship: Hartman cites Silencing the Past while questioning whether obeying historical conventions consigns captive girls to oblivion.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Venus2008,9–10/n32 cites Trouillot alongside StephanPalmié. The manufactured-certainties phrase belongs to Palmié94; Trouillot is a see-also resource, not source of every sentence or sole origin of critical fabulation. Complete article11–14 insists on restraint, irrecoverability and failure; not restoration of otherwise unknowable voices. Her cited1997 manifestation is retained.

proposals.relationship: Stoler uses Trouillot’s account of archival power to examine how histories are authorized and silenced.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Stoler2002,93/n24 pairs Trouillot with DavidW.Cohen, and96/n38 explicitly cites Trouillot55 on previous understandings/archivalpower.98/n49 adds a particular reference. Stoler’s NetherlandsIndies research and other analytical sources remain her own distinct intervention; not claim Trouillot founded the whole archival turn.

proposals.relationship: Trouillot questions the dismissal of an excess of history when a narrative of resistance can be necessary for Black students.
proposals.evidence_note: Own70–72 autobiographical teaching vignette explicitly says Nietzsche was wrong while reconsidering his own response to a student. Prefacexxii says he sensed an overdose of history long before reading UntimelyMeditations; no childhood influence inferred. Particular reflective disagreement, not fresh reconstruction or blanket rejection of Nietzsche’s philosophy.
